title: Manitou Hill
summary: Manitou Hill, also recorded as Mannatto, is the Manetto Hill ridge area in Plainview/Oyster Bay. The placename is connected with a 1695 deed and interpreted through the Manitto, or Great Spirit, tradition.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Matinecock Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: According to an oral history recorded in 1874, a sachem guided by the spirit force Manitou fired an arrow from this Plainview hill to miraculously locate a freshwater spring during a severe drought. Acknowledging such sacred geographies highlights how Algonquian belief systems intricately wove spiritual reverence together with a deep, practical reliance on the local environment.
introduction_content: Manitou Hill is associated with what is now known as Manetto Hill in Plainview, New York. The place-name record includes the related form Mannatto for Manetto Hill and connects the name with a 1695 Oyster Bay deed boundary. Later writers preserved story traditions and interpretations connected with Manitou, spring water, and the ridge landscape.
history_content: Manitou Hill carries both place-name and later story traditions connected with Manetto Hill in Plainview. Time-specific source details are separated into the Historic Moments below.
legends_and_lore_content:
In 1874, a reference to Manitou Hill and Long Island folklore comes from historian Gabriel Furman, who recounted a legend associated with what later was called Manetto Hill in Plainview, Long Island; 1
During a great drought, Manitou instructed a sachem, perhaps in a dream or through an intermediary, to stand on Manetto Hill and fire an arrow into the air. On the spot where the arrow landed, said the spirit message, the people should dig until they found water. The sachem did as he was told, and the arrow landed at the foot of the hill in a hollow.
There was a pond at the foot of the hill called "Mascopas," according to local historians Iris and Alonzo Gibbs, which is under the athletic field of John F. Kennedy High School 1.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Mannatto, Manetto, and Mannatto-adchu-auke. The name is analyzed through manitto, the Great Spirit; adchu, mountain or hill; and auke, land or country, giving the sense of Great Spirit mountain land.

Why Place Names Matter

“The restoration of an Aboriginal name to be used officially provides recognition to the Aboriginal name and assists in reawakening the language of that area.”

— Landgate, Government of Western Australia, Aboriginal place naming (2026), section 'What is Aboriginal naming?'
